Name this colorfully named 2004 to 2005 revolution in Ukraine.

The Arnolfini Wedding portrait was looted in the retreat from this battle, having earlier been stolen by the loser as his regime collapsed in the country where this battle took place. A preoccupation with evacuating spoils meant that the winner of this battle captured 152 artillery pieces--though he characteristically complained "We have in the service the scum of the earth as common soldiers" after his own troops looted rather than pursued the retreating enemy. The strategic aim of this battle was to cut off the retreat available to forces that had taken refuge in Burgos, which this battle's winning commander had tried and failed to capture the previous year, and a key element of the fighting prevented a withdrawal to Bilbao. Name this decisive 1813 battle of the Peninsular War, celebrated by Beethoven's Battle Symphony, in which Joseph Bonaparte was defeated by the then-Marquess of Wellington just outside a city in the Basque country.

One late-19th-century conflict in this present-day country pitted Pong Tiku of the Pangala against the Bone people in the Coffee War, in which the colonial power eventually intervened, executing Tiku and subjecting his Torajan people to the rule of the rival Bugis. In 1609, the orang kaya, an oligarchy in one part of this modern country, tricked colonial naval officers into appearing at a conference on Bandanaira, only to be murdered--an act that was reciprocated in spades in 1621 when a squadron under Jan Pieterszoon Coen massacred almost the entire population of the Banda Islands, leaving only enough survivors to cultivate its endemic clove trees on newly-introduced plantations. Name this modern country, whose independence movement involved collaborating with a Japanese invasion to overthrow centuries of Dutch domination.

Members of this group claimed to be descended from the ancient race of Sarmatians. The passage of "Nihil novi" strengthened their position, as it prevented any new laws from being made without their approval. Their power was further increased through the Henrician Articles, which required all kings of these people to be elected and remain accountable to them. After the Pact of Horodlo, Lithuanian boyars were given the same privileges as these people. Those privileges included liberum veto, the ability of any of these people to nullify any measures passed during a session of their political council. Name this class of people who lost much of their power after their commonwealth's partition.

Though this polity isn't Serbia, a resistance movement called the Black Hand operated here after the "Cement Incident" revealed large-scale arms shipments to this polity, and the killing of that group's leader Sheikh al- Qassam was the trigger for a major uprising against this entity's immigration policies. Concessions made to temper the uprising in turn led to a November 1938 protest in Oxford, motivated by policy intransigence in the aftermath of Kristallnacht. The assassination of Folke Bernadotte was an attempt to undermine one plan for partitioning this polity, which was created as a compromise between the Sykes-Picot Treaty and promises made by T.E. Lawrence. Name this colonial entity created by the League of Nations to administer a certain region, which lasted from 1922 until 1948 when the state of Israel was declared.

This treaty was preceded by the similar papal bull Inter caetara, which did not mention one of the parties to this treaty, and its implications were rejected on philosophical grounds by Francisco de Vitoria. It was negotiated along with the formation of the First Holy League to oppose French domination of Italy, a part of the diplomatic strategy of Alexander VI. The party harmed by this treaty provided funding for the War of the League of Cognac as part of a later settlement following contact with the Moluccas in 1521, which granted it nominal control it never exercised over the Philippines; that settlement was the Treaty of Zaragoza, which extended the principle of this treaty. Name this 1494 treaty that established a meridian dividing control of the non-European western hemisphere between Portugal and Spain.

Thomas Jones was one controversial nominee to the board of this institution, since he had served as a corporate director of the International Harvester Company, which at the time of his appointment was under indictment for illegal combination in restraint of trade. Benjamin Strong was an influential member of this institution, and his 1928 death was seen as historically pivotal by Charles Kindleberger and Milton Friedman. Senator Nelson Aldrich offered an early plan for this institution, which differed from the eventual result by using re-discounting of commercial paper as the mechanism by which this institution carried out its main function and by denying the President the power to appoint its board. Name this institution whose other controversial nominees include Peter Diamond, which uses open market operations to set monetary policy in the United States.

This man lost a Senate election to an incumbent found to be having an affair with Miss USA competitor Tai Collins after that state's other senator endorsed Marshall Coleman. When asked about a fence at his home, this man answered with a non-sequitur about challenging Abu Nidal anywhere in the world, and in another incident promised to tell all "the good, the bad, and the ugly." Eugene Hasenfus's plane was shot down while working for this man and Richard Secord's company, Project Democracy. His secretary Fawn Hill shredded "problem memos" after the Justice Department began investigating possible circumvention of the Boland Amendment. Name this "first five-star lieutenant colonel in the history of the military" who was brought before the Tower Commission for his involvement in the Iran-Contra Affair.

One man with this surname demanded that the federal budget for 1965 be under $100 billion as a condition for allowing the Kennedy/Johnson administration's income tax cuts to be voted through his Finance committee without amendment. A different senator by this name failed to deliver his crucial home state to Hubert Humphrey in the 1960 Democratic primary, which derailed that senator's strategy of using the Protestant Humphrey to knock off John Kennedy in favor of Lyndon Johnson. Both senators supported the southern manifesto, and the former advocated "Massive Resistance" to integration. The latter became infamous for the pork-barrel spending available to the Chairman of the Appropriations Committee. What is this surname shared by numerous Virginian and West Virginian senators?

John Conry adopted the Poughkeepsie model in creating one of these places in Faribault, Minesota. Many more were created after Sophia Shepard beat the ten-year-old Thomas Whall for over 30 minutes. The Bennett law angered Germans in Wisconsin by requiring these institutions to conduct affairs in English. Governor Walter Pierce was the defendant in two Supreme Court cases that overturned an Oregon law create to eliminate these places. James Blaine proposed an amendment that would prevent state funding of them. Hugo Black argued that a "general program" of services like fire protection or public transportation for people attending these was constitutional in Everson v. New Jersey. Warren Burger opined that laws in Pennsylvania and Rhode Island that supplemented salaries of people working in these places were unconstitutional, and created a three-part test for further government dealings with them in Lemon v. Kurtzman. Name these educational institutions.

William Capron consulted on this island's agricultural development and is thus responsible for its most famous export thanks to his introduction of American wheat and rye. Shakushain's revolt, a conflict that took place on this island in the late 17th century, was an uprising by the native population against settlers from the Matsumae clan, who had been granted control over this island and other concessions with the obligation to prevent an invasion originating from the Ainu living here. The short-lived Ezo Republic was set up on this island by the remnant of the Tokugawa Shogunate, before falling to the Imperial party in the final phase of the Boshin War. This island was then effectively annexed and developed in the face of the Russian threat during the Meiji period. Name this northernmost island of Japan.

This man intervened against the "Trojan" party in an internecine academic struggle at Oxford, as they were opposed to the study of the ancient literature this man promoted. This man was accused of colluding with Elizabeth Barton, to which his successful defense was a letter he'd written warning her off politics. This man's victims included Thomas Bilney and James Bainham, and his agents raided the home of Humphrey Monmouth as part of his campaign against the network that proliferated a book "printed in Utopia," a joke at this man's expense in the printer's mark of William Tyndale's translation of the Bible. Name this Lord Chancellor whose politically motivated 1536 execution occurred when he refused to recognize the King's authority over the Church of England.

"Shamefaced Crocians" was a phrase used to describe some of this group's members who had been disillusioned by the Action Party. The 1973 Chilean coup prompted the "historic compromise" between them and their country's ruling party. That compromise was initiated by a leader who with Georges Marchais and Santiago Carillo tried to distance themselves from the Soviet Union through the Eurocommunist movement. Another leader encouraged workers to support national, and not "self-styled class" interests in a speech delivered in Salerno. One of this group's founders argued the working class needed to achieve cultural hegemony before political in works published as his Prison Notebooks. Name this political party that split from the Socialists under Antonio Gramsci.

One man who took this name was briefly Archbishop of Rheims before he was stripped of his position by Pope John XV, who declared that his predecessor Arnulf's deposition was unlawful. The third pope who took on this name was excommunicated by Benedict IX and was deprived of his bishopric of Sabina at the Council of Sutri, and his original name was Giovanni dei Crescenzi. Another man of this name, with a feast day on New Years' Eve, supposedly cured a Roman emperor of leprosy with holy water on his way to becoming the recipient of the Donation of Constantine. That man was represented by Vitus and Vincentius at an ecumenical council that he himself did not physically attend, the First Council of Nicaea. The most famous pope of this name helped Hugh Capet to power and was placed on the throne by Emperor Otto II, and his name was Gerbert d'Aurillac. Give this name that belonged to three popes, including the first French pope, who also crowned Stephen I of Hungary.

This king sent massive tributes to Delphi after it correctly knew that this king had boiled a lamb and tortoise together in a bronze cauldron, and this ruler was the fifth in the Mermnad line of kings begun by king Gyges, who married the widow of king Candaules. This ruler formed alliances with Amasis II in Egypt and Nabonidus in Babylon. In one instance, this king welcomed the exiled Phrygian prince Adrastus, who accidentally killed this king's son Atys during a hunt. This king had a conversation with Solon of Athens about happiness during which Solon named Tellus the Athenian the world's most fortunate man. This ruler was warned to flee when a mule became the king of the Medians, and was again warned that a great empire would be destroyed if he crossed the Halys River, which resulted in his own army being destroyed by Persia. Name this king of Lydia whose empire was destroyed by Cyrus the Great and who was known for his massive wealth.

The quickness to take revenge for this action was encouraged by the deposed mayor Nicholas Bayard. One party involved in suppressing this event was delayed after his ship the Archangel struck rocks on Bermuda during the winter. Abrham de Peyster was an early supporter of this event, and after this event Benjamin Fletcher was made governor. This event was not supported by mayor Peter Schuyler, but gained strength when Indians destroyed Schenectady. Major Richard Ingoldesby ended this rebellion after the late arrival of governor Henry Sloughter, and he executed this rebellion's leader alongside his son-in-law Jacob Milbourne. This rebellion opposed lieutenant governor Francis Nicholson and the royal governor Sir Edmund Andros. Name this uprising against English authority in colonial New York after its namesake German captain learned of the Glorious Revolution.

Locations prominent in this battle included Kozlowski's Ranch and Raton Pass. One commander during this battle was informed of a supply train by Manuel Chaves and drove five hundred horses away from Johnson's Ranch, forcing the enemy to retreat. The campaign prior to this battle intended to access gold and silver mines and included the Battle of Valverde. During this battle, Charles Pyron commanded a regiment of Texans and Henry Hopkins Sibley attempted to take Fort Craig prior to this battle. William Scurry commanded one force during this battle along the Pecos River. During this battle, a force under John Slough and John Chivington held a position in the Sangre de Cristo Mountains southeast of Santa Fe. Name this "Gettysburg of the West," an 1862 battle in New Mexico that ended Confederate excursions into the American Southwest.

The second of these conflicts began when two British officers were murdered by Dewan Mulraj. The months leading up to these conflicts saw the victor at the Battle of Miani send home a telegram with the word "Peccavi," Latin for "I have sinned," shortly after taking Hyderabad. That conquest of Sindh by Sir Charles Napier led one side in these wars to launch a preemptive attack that was turned back by Sir Hugh Gough at the Battle of Mudki, and that conflict was ended when Gough defeated Rajas Tej and Lal at the Battle of Sobraon. The resulting Treaty of Lahore lasted only until Sher Singh Attariwalla crossed the Chenab River to attack the British at Ramnagar, but peace was restored at the Battle of Gujrat. This pair of conflicts was ended by the annexation of the Punjab by the British and the disbanding of the Khalsa Army. Name these wars fought between the British East India Company and members of a religion that reveres the Adi Granth.

In the middle of this conflict, William Gore Ouseley and Baron Deffaudis were sent to lead peace negotiations. One action in this war involved the Irish born admiral William Brown. Later flare-ups stemming from this conflict included the Revolution of the Lances and the uprising of Aparicio Saravia, and the most famous action of this conflict was preceded by the Battle of Arroyo Grande and was called "a new Troy" by Alexandre Dumas. The Sociedad Compradora was a central customs house in operation during this conflict. One side in this conflict wore blue armbands but replaced them with red ones after they faded in the sun, and this conflict featured opposing forces led by Manuel Oribe and Fructuoso Rivera. Featuring the participation of Giuseppe Garibaldi, this conflict included a five year long naval blockade by a joint British-French force. Name this conflict from 1839 to 1851 between the Colorados and Blancos in a certain South American country on the Rio de la Plata.

The dissent to this court case cited West Virginia State Board of Education v. Barnette in explaining a freedom from "embarrassments and pleasures" and also cited the fourth stanza of the "Star Spangled Banner." The precedent established in this case was later upheld in Abington v. Schempp and Lee v. Weisman, which involved a guest speaker at a Rhode Island middle school. The majority opinion in this case mentioned the historical persecution of John Bunyan and commented on the briefness of a twenty-two word statement opposed by a group which included the Ethical Culture movement. Byron White took no part in the case and Felix Frankfurter had suffered a stroke which resulted in a 6-1 decision. The opinion in this case was delivered by Hugo Black and stated that the items in question violated the Establishment Clause, and the case was brought about by Jewish associations in New York. Name this 1962 supreme court decision which stated that forced recitation of prayer in public schools was unconstitutional.

This future emperor gained favor after winning a poetry contest in which he completed the line "wind blows the horse's tail into a thousand strands of thread," with the line, "sun reflects off the dragons' scales into ten thousand bits of gold." This emperor feigned mental illness while plotting to take over the Jianwen Emperor, and this ruler ordered a costly attack against the Tatar king Arughtai. During this emperor's reign, Le Loi revolted in Vietnam and established the Le Dynasty. This emperor widened the Grand Canal and a namesake encyclopedia was compiled during his reign. He chose Tianshou Mountain as the site of the Ming Tombs which would include the burial sites of thirteen emperors, and this emperor commissioned the naval voyages of the eunuch Zheng He. Taking a name meaning "perpetual happiness," name this third emperor of the Ming Dynasty who moved the capital to Beijing and built the Forbidden City.

Jury instructions during this event included a warning not to "rivet the chains of bondage on your own necks"; as a result, James Maury was awarded only a single penny of damages in his suit at the Hanover County courthouse. Controversial aspects of this event included the fact that the presiding judge and defense lawyer were father and son, and John Camm's decision to appeal to the Privy Council. A speech given during this event accused the king of degenerating "into a tyrant" who forfeits "all rights to his subjects' obedience." It was sparked by a 1758 drought that raised the price of tobacco, prompting the passage of the Two Penny Act to substitute cash for debts ordinarily paid in tobacco, such as the salaries of Virginia's Anglican clergymen. FTP, name this controversy that advanced the early political career of Patrick Henry.

Peter Clarke's book about the "last thousand days of" this wondered if it had ended in a "scuttle." Argentina was informally incorporated into this polity until the rise of Juan Manuel de Rosas, according to the "free trade" interpretation of it proposed by Cambridge historians John Gallagher and Ronald Robinson. Antoinette Burton's study of travellers "at the heart of" this place examines Cornelia Sorabji's journey across it to attend medical school. J.R. Seeley famously wrote that it had been acquired "in a fit of absence of mind." Historians often divide this entity into a "first" one based on Atlantic commerce and the slave trade, and a "second" one that resulted in direct rule over India and much of Africa, a process sometimes called "painting the map red." FTP, name this colonial structure on which "the sun never set."

This politician first gained prominence when, despite initial controversy caused by his background as an infantry officer, he was an effective chief of the Navy. Prior to losing power over a failed attempt to legalize religious boarding schools, this man's government gained control of the Fwe People and renounced his claims to the Wituland Sultanate. Via that same treaty, which was part of his "New Course" foreign policy that emphasized good relations with Western Europe rather than Russia, this man obtained control of Heligoland but agreed to allow British intervention in Zanzibar. Name this man who succeeded Otto von Bismarck as Chancellor of Germany, perhaps most famous for his namesake strip in Africa.

Operation Earnest Will was an American naval convoy during this war. Tensions flared during this war when an American-flagged tanker, the Bridgeton, struck a mine, leading the United States to carry out anti-mine patrols and sink mine-laying ships. During this war, the USS Stark was nearly sunk by missiles from a single fighter jet. The frigate Sahand was sunk during a US Navy hunt for its sister ship, the notorious Sabalan, during this war. During this war, the United States destroyed oil fields in Operation Praying Mantis and the USS Vincennes used its AEGIS missile system to shoot down a civilian airliner. Name this 1980's war notable for the use of chemical weapons by then-US ally Saddam Hussein against Ayatollah Khomeni.

General James Ledlie was dismissed from service for spending this battle drinking rum in a bombproof shelter. Ledlie's troops, who led the initial confused assault on "Elliott's Salient" during this battle, had been last- minute replacements for Edward Ferrero's division of United States Colored Troops. Many of Ferrero's men, sent in to restore order, were executed or returned to slavery by the victors, who were led by a future Readjuster Party senator from Virginia, William Mahone. Preparations for this battle were made by Henry Pleasants, whose 48th Pennsylvania regiment, recruited from Schuylkill County coal miners, planted "320 kegs of gunpowder" in the tunnel they dug under the Confederate trenches. FTP, name this July 1864 battle, in which Union forces tried to end the siege of Petersburg with a giant explosion.

Desmond Morton has been accused of leaking this document, whose dispatch was confirmed by "an individual in touch with M. Rakovsky and the Arcos Bank." Proposed originators of this document include Uexkull, a Baltic-German forger; Druzhelovski, who supposedly transmitted it to Polish intelligence; and Bellegarde, a White Russian emigre whose widow Irina wrote to the Sunday Times that she had watched her late husband forge it. A delegation from the Trades Union Congress that visited Moscow found no archival evidence for this document, which called for hastening the "liberation of the British proletariat." The head of the Comintern who formed a troika with Kamenev and Stalin supposedly signed, FTP, what controversial letter that brought down Ramsay MacDonald's first Labour government?

The first named member of this group was one D'Arcy Boulton senior, who made his son of the same name Master of Chancery and his son William a professor at King's College. Other key members included the attorney-general who presided over the Ancaster show trial, John Beverley Robinson, and the Scottish-born bishop who sat "at the ear of his Majesty's representative like the serpent at the ear of Eve in Paradise," John Strachan. According to an article in the Colonial Advocate, this group was "a dozen of nobodies" who relied on patronage and pensions for their absolute power. This group, the upriver analogue of James McGill's Château Clique, infuriated rebels who met at Montgomery's Tavern under the leadership of William Lyon Mackenzie. FTP, what supposedly nepotistic rulers of Anglophone Canada were targeted by the rebellion of 1837?

A document published by this group complained about the imprisonment of Major Tulidah, the oppressions of the Merchant Adventurers monopoly, and the existing government's continuation of religious persecution once carried out by the High Commission. That document was called Gold Tried in the Fire because it responded to the public burning of this group's petitions. An early mutiny by this group took place on Corkbush Field near Ware; a later one ended when three of the ringleaders were shot in a churchyard at Burford. One leader of this movement was stabbed at Doncaster by conspirators who tried to capture him in exchange for Marmaduke Langdale. That man, who was told "you must fly for refuge to an absolute natural right" by Henry Ireton, was Colonel Thomas Rainsborough, an opponent of the "grandees" at the Putney Debates. Members of this movement wore sea-green ribbons to protest the imprisonment of the author of England's New Chains Discovered, John Lilburne. FTP, identify this movement from the English Revolution, named for its platform of flattening all social distinction.

Late in life this woman engaged in a heated lawsuit with a Scottish doctor named Stewart, who was accused of embezzling the fortune entrusted to support her in her retirement. After the end of her disastrous marriage to the French army surgeon Xavier Quatrefages, this woman fled to Paris and supported herself as an "Instructress in Languages." She left Paris on board the gunboat Tacuari, whose hold contained sets of Limoges and Sevres china and a grand piano. Dressed in a "ragged ballgown," she dug the graves of her eldest son Panchito and his father with her bare hands. Her kindness to Major da Cunha Matos, who had been captured at the Battle of Tuyuti, helped ensure that she too would receive decent treatment from the Brazilians who seized her at Cerro Corá after she and her family were forced to flee from Asunción. Lily Tuck's novel The News from Paraguay fictionalizes the life of, FTP, what Irish-born mistress of Francisco Solano López?

The first king with this name came to power by overthrowing his brother, Andrew I, and was nicknamed "the Bison". The second king of this name ruled for ten years despite being blinded as a child. The fourth king of this name was nicknamed "the second founder of the country" because of his response to the Tatarjaros. That king lost the battle of Mohi to Subotai, saw much of his domain ravaged by the Mongols, causing him to move the royal residence from Szekesfehervar to the more defendable Buda. Followers of one politician with this name were condemned in the "Arraignment Speech", delivered in front of the Gellert Hotel by Miklos Horthy, and were targeted in the Hungarian White Terror. That politician had founded a short-lived Soviet Republic after World War I. Give this common Hungarian name shared by Communist leader Kun and famous composer Bartok.

During one war, this navy deployed the "Sea Quake", a speedboat armed with depth charges that was often unable to survive the explosions it caused. This navy was expanded after hawks adopted the "Eight-Eight Doctrine". An Englishman named William Forbes-Sempill introduced sea planes to this navy. During World War I, this navy captured the German port of Tsingtao in China. This navy supported amphibious landings on Kiska and Attu. One of this navy's losses led to the cancellation of Operation Mo. In another battle, this navy took substantial losses because its carriers were attacked while planes were refueling. Name this navy that lost the Battle of Midway, led by Admiral Yamamoto.

This clause was broadened in the cases Lucas v. South Carolina Coastal Council and Hawaii Housing Authority v. Midkiff. An influential interpretation of this clause was the 1954 case Berman v. Parker, which declared the District of Columbia Redevelopment Act to be constitutional. A recent controversial case that broadened this clause was Kelo v. City of New London, which determined that economic development qualifies as a "public use". Name this last clause of the Fifth Amendment, which states that the titular action cannot be performed "without just compensation."

One site believed to belong to this people is Tilla Tepe, which includes this people's distinctive gold jewelry. Strabo described these people as being located beyond Bactria and Sogdiana, and described how they were also known as Daheans. Herodotus described how this people described themselves as being founded by Targitaus, the son of the sky-god, and argues that this people probably moved west after battling with the Massagetae. This people was known as the Sacas in Indian records, and their confederations included the Amyrgians in the east and the Sarmatians of the west. This people is best known for its burial mounds known as kurgans, and the presence of armed women among this people may have inspired the story of Amazons. Name these Iranian peoples who lived north of the Black Sea.

Sackville Carden was forced to draw up a purely naval version of this plan, and was replaced by John de Robeck. This operation was ended by Charles Monro, of whom it was written "he came, he saw, he capitulated." The attackers in this engagement failed to take "The Narrows" and were defeated at engagements like the Battle of the Nek and the Battle of Lone Pine, both part of the August Offensive. Key locations in this campaign included Helles, Suvla Bay, and Anzac Cove, named for the many Australians and New Zealanders who participated. Name this disastrous 1915-1916 World War I campaign, the brainchild of Winston Churchill, in which the Allies invaded Turkey.

The original homeland of this people was known as the Etelköz, from which this people was driven after defeat in the Battle of Southern Buh by the Pechenegs. That defeat came after this people allied with Leo the Wise of the Byzantine Empire to fight King Simeon I of Bulgaria, and resulted in the ritual sacrifice of this people's leader. That leader's successor became the namesake of a dynasty of this people which included Bela IV, who led this people's rebuilding after invasion by the Mongols. This people's most famous leader received recognition of this people's independence from the Holy Roman Empire from Pope Silvester II and Emperor Otto III in the form of a crown, which became known as his namesake Holy Crown. Name these nomads led by Arpad and Saint Steven, the ancestors of the modern Hungarian people.

This city is the subject of the Dongan Charter, the oldest city charter still in force in the United States. Thurlow Weed named one group named after this city which was originally made up of the leaders of a group named the Bucktails before later being known as Hunkers. That group named after this city which battled the Barnburners coined the term "to the victors go the spoils" and one of its leaders was Martin Van Buren. A meeting named after this city began as a treaty negotiation with the Mohawks and was the subject of a poster featuring a chopped up snake with the caption "Join or Die." name this city that was the namesake of a "Regency" as well as of a Congress to discuss American unification.

One incident involving this man saw members of his group including Pete Pierpoint and Charles Makley break him out of a jail in Lima, Ohio after pretending to be State Police officers sent to extradite him. This man and several members of his group were apprehended in one instance after firefighters identified members of his group after a fire at the Hotel Congress where they were staying. That incident was followed in one in which this man escaped a prison in Crown Point by carving a pistol out of a block of wood. This figure was killed after attending the play Manhattan Melodrama and his occurred after Ana Cumpănaş agreed to become the Woman in Red in order to point him out. Name this bank robber who was shot by FBI agents outside the Biograph Theater and who was the subject of rumors that he actually escaped.

A companion charter to the Magna Carta gave common people rights to access these. Management practices of these in 19th century Germany meant to maximize the production levels of these ironically led these to be so unproductive that Germans coined a word to describe the death of these. One of the most important practitioners of a discipline studying these argued for the damming of the Hetch Hetchy Valley against John Muir. That man, Gifford Pinchot, endowed a school for the study of of these at Yale. Theodore Roosevelt federally protected 150 of these while in office. Name these areas that are hurt by Waldsterben, some of which are extracted from by companies like Weyerhaeuser and Plum Creek Timber.

Two rulers of this name, including one known as the first Renaissance monarch of his nation, are featured in the Trinity Altarpiece by Hugo van der Goes. Forces loyal to one of those rulers of this name were victorious at the Battle of Lochmaben Fair, while the other of those rulers of this name was forced to declare war under the terms of the Auld Alliance after the beginning of the War of the League of Cambrai, resulting in a battle in which his army's pikes were defeated by the bills of the enemy, the Battle of Flodden Field. Another ruler of this name wrote a book on witch hunting known as Daemonologie as well as the works on kingship Basilikon Doron and The True Law of Free Monarchies. Name this name shared by seven Scottish monarchs, including the first Stuart king of England.

The death of labor leader Ginger Goodwin in this province was the impetus for Canada's first general strike. Anthony Musgrave presided over the entrance of this province into the Dominion of Canada, an effort which was supported by the Confederation League. Due to the French Revolution, France notably decided not to intervene in tensions between Spain and Great Britain over encounters off of Nootka Sound in this modern day province. Arthur "Slim" Evans began the "On to Ottawa" Trek in this province, the largest city of which was founded after the merger of the Hudson's Bay and North West companies. That city was named after a figure who visited the Strait of Juan de Fuca, though he failed to discover the Columbia River. Name this Canadian province home to Vancouver.

The best-known battle from this war began after three women secretly planted bombs in a milk bar where young people were dancing. In a failed attempt to end this conflict, a famous general incorrectly and ambiguously cried, "I have understood you!" One side in this conflict created a 200-mile electric fence called the Morice Line. After its end, the harkis had to flee or risk being lynched. Towards the end of this conflict, a group of generals defied their country by forming the Secret Army Organization to kill more of their enemies. This conflict rapidly lost popularity due to the brutal torture tactics authorized by General Massu, which were documented in a film by Gillo Pontecorvo. This conflict was ended by the Evian Accords, which effectively required the pied-noirs to evacuate and gave victory to Ahmed Ben Bella and the FLN. Name this conflict that ruined the French Fourth Republic and gave independence to North African colony.

This ruler put down the revolt of the Dalecarlians in Dalarna, where he got support from local copper miners. This winner at Brunnbäck Ferry appointed the Petri brothers to religious office. His high taxes led rebelling peasants to use crossbows under the leadership of Nils Dacke. This man's deeds were the subject of a Henry Brooke play banned by the UK's 1737 Licensing Act because Robert Walpole saw the play as a satire on him. In real life, this man unified his country before signing the Treaty of Malmo. This king exiled Gustav Trolle, an archbishop who had this king's father killed in a 1520 bloodbath, and converted his country to Lutheranism after freeing it from the Kalmar Union. Name this king of a newly-independent Sweden, the founder of a namesake dynasty whose later members included Gustavus Adolphus.

One kingdom of this name sent troops south through mountains on the Stone Cattle Road after promising their hapless opponents that they would use the trail to deliver cows made of stone that defecated gold. A later polity known by this name adopted black flags and black armor after a declaration that it was "ruled by the power of water;" that polity featured a court purge after its leader and several officials refused to call a deer a horse, and built a roadway system encompassing the Ordos Loop under general Meng Tian. This state built the Min river's Dujiangyan irrigation facility, and Huhai of this dynasty was forced to kill himself by the eunuch Zhao Gao. The dynasty of this name standardized "small-seal script" among the mandates of Han Fei and Li Si, two unrepentant Legalists, and lost its founder to mercury poisoining. Name this state which burned the books after coming out on top in the Warring States period, declaring itself a dynasty under the immortality- seeking Shi Huangdi.

One king of these people held a religious council at Agde and put a royal rescript in front of a legal code for a non-ruling ethnic majority called the Breviary. The legal distinction between these people and that subject majority was ended by a twelve-book code, the Book of the Judges. King Wamba ruled these people a century and a half after religious changes ended rule by their "bold men," or Balti, dynasty. One nobleman of these people led his army out of a cave and into a narrow valley to defeat Munuza's troops and kill al-Qama. This people used one set of bishops and tolerated another, switching their favor when Reccared converted to Catholicism from Arianism. This ethnic group won out at Covadonga under Pelayo. After losing at Vouillé, they lost their Gallic possessions to Clovis's Franks and stayed in Spain. Name this barbarian people who started the Reconquista three hundred years after their leader Alaric sacked Rome.

This state's DOI-CODI tortured journalist Vladimir Herzog to death for his associations with communism. It contains a cluster of three automotive industry centers called the ABC Region. In this state's capital, guards massacred 111 rioting inmates of Carandiru Prison. This state was the launching ground for expeditions of explorers called bandeirantes who sought to enslave the native population. This state's nomination of Julio Prestes for the presidency in 1930 broke a deal it had made to alternate control of the presidency with a dairy-producing neighbor. The site of the Week of Modern Art, this state shared power with Minas Gerais during the Coffee with Milk period and retained some of its independence during the Estado Novo. Name this most populous and wealthiest state in Brazil.

This colony was home to the battle of Ramsour's Mill, and a switch of leaders in it led to Carey's Rebellion. One native leader in this colony was recognized by whites as King Tom Blunt. Two armies in this polity engaged in the "Race for the Dan," a chase ending at Cowan's Ford, decades after it was home to a siege of indigenous people at Fort Neohoroka. This polity was the destination of an Indian-killing expedition led by John Barnwell. Its leaders included Charles Eden, who took money from pardoned yet still-active pirates. One movement in this colony objected to this usage of public funds on a palace at New Bern for Governor William Tryon, but fell apart after fighting at Alamance Creek. Name this colony from which the Tuscarora fled, which was home to the Regulator Movement and Guilford Courthouse after the splitting an earlier British province.

According to one story, this man once cursed two friars who wished him peace, declaring, "I live on war, and peace will undo me." Catherine of Siena once sent an embassy of three men demanding that this man end his war with Pisa and go on crusade. After his enemy Konrad von Landau had his nose smashed in by a rock, this man, along with Albert Sterz, routed the Great Company at the Battle of Canturino. This man lost a battle celebrated in a Michelangelo cartoon, the Battle of Cascina. His less noble ventures include committing the massacres of Faenza and Cesena. Gregory XI hired this man to put down the revolts of the Papal States during the War of the Eight Saints. This leader of the White Company is celebrated in a "funerary monument" created by Paolo Uccello. Name this English condottiero who repeatedly switched sides in 14th-century Italy.

One of these locales was simulated in the Bull Ring at Etaples. The Nahkampfmesser and the so-called "French Nail" were designed for use in these locations, which are preserved by museums at Dixmude and Sanctuary Wood. A ritual sometimes called the "morning hate" was carried out daily in these locales. A force called the Patricias devised a way to target these locations stealthily in raids, a signature of the Canadian Corps. Between the battle of Aigne and the Battle of Yser, a "race to the sea" began the most famous usage of these locales, which lend their name to a gangrenous swelling of the foot. The creation of these things is sometimes called sapping, and the command "over the top" was given to send men from these structures into "No Man's Land". Name these earthen structures along the Western Front of World War I.

The last surviving member of this military formation had hoboed his way to New York to enlist, only to have the unit's commander buy him a train ticket to Texas. That man is Jesse Langdon. The uniforms worn by this military unit were designed by Brooks Brothers, and Richard Davis described an incident where one member of this unit removed a stuck shell from a gun with an axe. Hamilton Fish II, a member of this unit, was killed fighting alongside Buffalo Soldiers under Joseph Wheeler at the Battle of Las Guasimas. Members of this unit held reunions in Panama, as its leader was visiting the Canal. In World War I, Congress authorized the recreation of this unit, but Woodrow Wilson opposed it. Name this military formation which, after Leonard Wood was promoted, stormed Kettle Hill and the San Juan Heights under the command of Theodore Roosevelt during the Spanish-American War.

Thomas Tipton served in between Congressional terms of one man by this name, who fired 40,000 Postal Workers of the opposing party when serving as Postmaster-General. Another person with this name defeated Ralph Smith to win election to the Senate, where he sponsored an amendment cutting off aid to Israel. Another man by this name worked on the Preparatory Commission of the United Nations Organizations and defeated Dwight Green in the 1948 election for governor of Illinois. One person by this name was William Jenning Bryan's Democratic running mate in 1900, and another person by this name died while ambassador to Great Britain, a post he held when John F. Kennedy appointed him there after defeating him in a Primary. Name this name shared by Grover Cleveland's second vice-president and his son, who lost to Eisenhower in the 1952 and 1956 Presidential elections.

This case was decided 20 years after the California State Supreme Court arrived at the same conclusion in Perez v. Sharp, and the New York State Supreme Court declined to use it as precedent in Hernandez v. Robles. A lower court decision in this case was written by Harry Carrico and cited Maynard v. Hill, while another judge quoted extensively from Johann Blumenbach. This case was preceded by the similar Naim v. Naim, although Naim was not appealed to the Supreme Court. This case, which was cited in Perry v. Brown, extended McLaughlin v. Florida, which applied to cohabitation, and overturned Pace v. Alabama. Name this 1968 Supreme Court that overturned state laws forbidding interracial marriage.

This event was largely the responsibility of a man who had previously appeared in advertisements for his employer, Jacob Veldhuyzen. A contributing factor to this event was radio heterodyne, which kept Veldhuyzen from hearing two messages. This event was indirectly caused by MPAIAC's planting of a bomb in a flower shop at Las Palmas, the original destination of its participants. This event was exacerbated by Veldhuyzen's insistence on fully refueling and destroyed the "Clipper Victor," the first Boeing 747 to enter service. Occurring when one participant was back-taxiing due to the only taxiway's being filled with other parked airplanes, it led to the introduction of standardized terminology, so that no plane would prematurely try to take off, and its participants could not see each other because of a heavy fog. Name this deadliest airplane accident, where a KLM Boeing 747 collided with a Pam Am 747 during take-off in the Canary Islands.

During this battle, John Cutts' forces captured two water mills. Henry Overkirk was assigned to guard a French attack shortly before this battle, which necessitated a march of over 21,000 men from Bedburg to the location of the battle. The "Wild Geese" brigade, which had previously fled from Ireland, participated in this battle under the command of the Marquis de Blainville. John Cutts led an early attack in this battle, which was preceded by one commander broke off the Siege of Villingen in preparation for this battle. It occurred on the Nebel River after Ferdinand de Martin and the Duke of Vendome threatened to capture Venice, and the Duke of Tallard was captured in this battle despite the reinforcements he brought. The Allied forces were commanded by Eugene of Savoy and John Churchill, Duke of Marlborough. Name this turning point of the War of the Spanish Succession.

One official of this government attempted to flee aboard the Rose, and appointed a man who disrespected members of the militia at Ft. James. One conflict in this polity started after a leader was misquoted as threatening to burn down a town in it. Edward Randolph held several posts early in this government's rule, and eventually had a falling out with its provisional head, Joseph Dudley. Escapades during this government's founding led to the name of Connecticut's Charter Oak. Abraham de Peyster supported the overthrow of Francis Nicholson by Leisler's Rebellion in part of this authority, part of which was briefly governed by the Albany Convention. Among this government's goals were enforcement of the Navigation Acts, and this government's overthrow was sparked by the Glorious Revolution. Name this consolidated colonial government once headed by Edmund Andros.

The term "Buffalo Hunt" never caught on for this activity, which caused the first expulsion from the U.S. Senate. The Amelia Island Affair resulted from Luis-Michel Aury doing this, and James Long was the last person to attempt it in Texas. George Mathews attempted this in East Florida with U.S. Government complicity, and in the 1830s members of "Hunters' Lodges" participated in this activity around the Great Lakes. The Costa Rican José María Cañas won the Battle of Rivas against one practitioner of this activity, who tried to found a "Republic of Sonora" and briefly ruled Nicaragua. That man, William Walker, was a Nashville native attempting to expand U.S. Slave territory in Latin America through this enterprise. Name this activity in which American citizens independently sought to conquer territories and adjoin them to the United States, which lends its name to an obfuscatory parliamentary procedure.

This state was the site of the Benxihu coal-mining disaster, and it employed a secret police force known as the Hoankyoku. It was the site of the Battle of Lake Khasan and of the Nomontan Incident, and its first Prime Minister, Zheng Xiaoxu, also composed its national anthem. Its statehood was denied by the Lytton Report, and it served as the main area of operations for the Kwantung Army. With its capital at Hsingking, the renamed Changchun, its head of state was the Kangde Emperor, and medical war crimes were committed by Unit 731 in Harbin in this state. Identify this state formed shortly after the Mukden incident and led by the figurehead Pu Yi, a Japanese puppet state in Manchuria.

The leader of this movement may have gained power using much brandy. A governor's monopoly on the beaver trade was attacked by a document of this event, which William Drummond was executed for his role in. This event's origins stem from Doeg Indians stealing hogs from Thomas Matthews and John Washington attacked a Susquehannock fort in the leadup to this event, during which the Burgesses voted to allow landless freemen to vote. The instigator of this event claimed that "We must defend ourselves against all the Indians" and Jamestown was burned down during this. Name this revolt against William Berkley in Virginia.

Moses of Khorene claimed certain rulers here were Davidic descendants. The Byzantines entrusted the Pahalvuni family with the rule of parts of here. One dynasty that ruled this country built a dynastic church on Akadamar and Trdat built several churches in its medieval capital at Ani. Nerses of Lambron supported union of its church with Rome, which happened under Lavon I. Queen Tamar of Georgia expelled the Shadaddids from here. This country's Hetum I allied with the Mongols and the Rubenids founded its Cilician incarnation. Name this country whose church was founded by Gregory the Illuminator, subject to Turkish ethnic cleansing in 1915, whose modern incarnation disputes Nagorno-Korbakh with Azerbajian.

This oration discusses a ten-dollar check which the speaker promises to "never cash" and a woman born on St. Patrick's Day who, like the speaker, is "not a quitter." Part of it questions Stephen Mitchell's assertion that only a rich man should run for Senate, and its speaker earlier noted that he did not pay a salary to his wife, unlike his counterpart John Sparkman. This speech listed completely a man's financial situation, explaining that "Pat" "doesn't have a mink coat" and why its speaker needed an eighteen-thousand dollar political fund. This speech saved its giver's spot on the Republican ticket, and was given eight years to the day after FDR's similarly-themed "Fala" speech. Identify this 1952 Richard Nixon speech in which he discussed his family's black and white cocker spaniel.

Plutarch quotes the physician Ctesias' description of one part of this battle in which Mithridates "struck a dart into" the temple of one side's commander, who then fell on a rock and died. Earlier, a subordinate commander in this battle had refused to move to the center so that the Euphrates could protect his right flank. Clearchus took command of one side's army after this battle, but was himself later murdered at a banquet given by Tissaphernes. According to one historian present, only one Greek mercenary was even wounded, though it was the final defeat in Cyrus the Younger's failed revolt against his brother Ataxerxes II. Identify this battle described in Xenophon's Anabasis, after which the Ten Thousand had to retreat back to Greece.
